question: What transformer depth and learned attention-head stack are needed for multi-step associative retrieval, and why does intermediate supervision enable the circuit to emerge?

key_findings.claim: The retrieval task extends induction by requiring D chained associations, while conditional retrieval permits a directed acyclic dependency graph.
key_findings.evidence: Inputs contain interleaved pairs forming chains from query x0 to target xD; five natural-language formulations test equations, cohabitation, fictional kingdoms, functions, and relatives.

key_findings.claim: Under a simplified information-sharing model, at least log base 3 of 2D transformer layers are required for the final position to retrieve xD.
key_findings.evidence: The proof bounds the amount of prerequisite information reachable at a position by a factor of three per layer, assuming attention is possible only between positions already sharing information and transfers all attended information.

key_findings.claim: The logarithmic theorem is conditional and does not establish an unconditional lower bound for standard softmax transformers.
key_findings.evidence: Attention can align through learned content beyond literal pre-existing shared information, and the analysis deliberately ignores capacity, masking, and training; Assumption 1 is the critical restriction producing the information-flow graph.

key_findings.claim: Intermediate targets create an implicit curriculum that is necessary for the reported synthetic training success.
key_findings.evidence: Across 64 one-to-eight-layer runs per formulation, every direct-target non-curriculum run for D=3 finishes above 0.7 MSE, whereas concatenated intermediate targets learn earlier chain positions first and deeper models solve later positions.

key_findings.claim: Three independently trained 12-layer one-head-per-layer transformers use sparse but non-minimal stacks of retrieval heads that share an induction-like first step and diverge afterward.
key_findings.evidence: All reach validation MSE below 0.01; manual attention-map analysis plus ablations finds four useful heads per model, though three suffice constructively, and later head paths differ across seeds.

key_findings.claim: Checkpoint analysis supports sequential circuit assembly: an induction head appears first and later heads reuse it to extend retrieval depth.
key_findings.evidence: In a 24-layer D=4 model, attention paths cross the 0.5 threshold in chain order after roughly 450 slow-learning epochs; partial losses fall in the corresponding order.

key_findings.claim: The prompted LLM results demonstrate behavioral capability but not that production models use the same manually recovered synthetic circuit.
key_findings.evidence: Several LLMs answer 500 generated items per formulation well for D up to five, but internal weights are not inspected and answer sampling is repeated until an acceptable format appears.

method.core_idea: Use chained associative retrieval as a depth-sensitive testbed, combine an information-flow lower bound with controlled training and manual attention-circuit reconstruction.
method.mechanism: Intermediate supervision exposes every chain prefix; an induction-like head first links pair tokens; subsequent heads attend through residual information produced by earlier heads, progressively extending the reachable chain.
assumptions: The theorem's attention graph requires positions to share information before attending.
Attending transfers all information and capacity limits can be ignored for the lower-bound argument.
Synthetic Gaussian symbol vectors and rotary positions isolate retrieval from semantic shortcuts.
Attention maps and ablation suffice to identify the useful circuit.
Intermediate-target supervision is a reasonable analogue of curricula present in natural language.

techniques.role: Creates a controllable reasoning chain that generalizes induction heads.
Relates reachable associations to transformer layer count.
Supervises all chain prefixes so useful heads can emerge sequentially.
Manually identifies head paths responsible for retrieval.
Measures when each circuit edge appears during optimization.

evaluations.setting: Five prompted retrieval/conditional-retrieval formulations, 500 random questions each, with multiple LLMs.
evaluations.metric: Exact acceptable-answer accuracy versus D and random guessing.
evaluations.result: Models perform strongly across formulations and nearly perfectly on equations through D=5, subject to answer-format resampling.
evaluations.baseline: Random guessing and increasing chain depth.

evaluations.setting: 128 transformers with one to eight layers, D=5 for IC and D=3 for direct target.
evaluations.result: All direct-target runs fail above 0.7 MSE; IC models learn positions in order and later positions require greater depth.

evaluations.setting: Three 12-layer one-head models at D=3 and one 24-layer model at D=4.
evaluations.metric: Validation MSE, ablation effect, attention paths, and path-emergence epoch.
evaluations.result: Sparse stacked-head circuits solve retrieval, differ across seeds after the first induction-like step, and emerge sequentially under IC.
evaluations.baseline: Unused heads, ablated circuits, and the theoretical minimal head count.

limitations: The depth theorem relies on a strong attention-sharing abstraction, not the full transformer model.
Synthetic trained models use explicit intermediate supervision absent from ordinary next-token objectives.
Circuit reconstruction is manual and covers only four trained models.
The recovered circuits are non-minimal and seed-dependent.
Prompted LLM behavior is not causally connected to the synthetic mechanism.
The emergence claim tracks attention thresholds rather than a full optimization theory.
failure_modes: Without intermediate targets, gradient descent fails to discover the stack even when depth is sufficient.
Too few layers prevent information propagation under the assumed graph.
Later heads cannot form before earlier residual information becomes available.
Attention-map inspection can miss distributed MLP or value-path computation.
Answer resampling can overestimate practical prompted reliability.
reusable_insights: Depth-sensitive synthetic tasks can separate representational capacity from optimization success.
Intermediate losses can reveal and scaffold the causal order in which multi-stage circuits form.
Circuit motifs may be shared while exact head locations and redundant paths vary across seeds.
A lower bound should state whether it applies to the architecture or to an auxiliary information-flow model.
open_questions: Can an unconditional transformer-depth lower bound be proved for retrieval?
Does ordinary next-token pretraining supply equivalent intermediate gradients, and on which corpus structures?
Can automated causal tracing recover the same stacked circuits across many seeds?
What is the minimum head/layer circuit under realistic masking and finite width?
Do LLMs use stacked induction heads or a different mechanism on semantic retrieval prompts?

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. identify two-head induction for A B ... A to B and its training phase change; the target extends the motif to D chained associations and observes sequential reuse by deeper head stacks.

competitive_landscape.title: Thinking Like Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Weiss et al. compile RASP programs into upper bounds on heads and layers and compare learned patterns; the target proposes a lower bound under an information-sharing model and studies head emergence.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: This work studies delayed generalization and systematicity of latent relation composition; the target focuses on contextual chain retrieval, explicit prefix supervision, and stacked attention paths.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: ACDC automates sparse graph discovery and validates known transformer circuits; the target manually reconstructs full small-model retrieval circuits and can be used as a benchmark for such automation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Retrieval supplies a depth-requiring task whose stacked attention circuit emerges one head at a time under an implicit curriculum.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A conditional lower bound, 128-run depth/curriculum sweep, three reverse-engineered circuits, and checkpoint path chronology support the account.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The sequential head-emergence study is a useful extension of induction-head work. The depth claim must remain explicitly conditional, and transfer from intermediate-supervised toys to pretrained LLMs is not established.
